archetype.name: Dual-Threat (pocket-first)
archetype.definition: A third-year passer who now wins mostly on schedule from the pocket with accurate short and middle-of-field throws, while his scrambles still bail out broken plays.

report.headline: The accuracy leap is real; the turnover spike is mostly one bad afternoon.
report.take:
For two years Caleb Williams was a talented but scattershot thrower. He ranked 53rd and 52nd in bad-throw rate, posted a negative CPOE both seasons, and was trusted more for his legs and his off-script plays than for hitting the routine throw. Through six starts in his second year under Ben Johnson, that profile has flipped. His completion rate is up 10.6 points on last season, his CPOE has jumped to 6.17 (7th of 54), and his bad-throw rate has fallen to 11.8% (6th of 42). He sits 10th in passing EPA per dropback at 0.166, almost two-tenths of a point above the league's qualifiers, and the Bears are 5-1 in his starts.

The engine is the short game. On throws of 0-9 air yards he completes 80.2% with 0.274 EPA per attempt and a 61.6% success rate, and that band produced more EPA than any other depth. Johnson's under-center looks help: Williams is more efficient under center (0.183) than in shotgun (0.102), and all five of his interceptions came from the gun. The middle of the field has been his best direction at 0.38 EPA a throw. Rome Odunze has been the explosive outlet, turning only 28 targets into 0.742 EPA per target, far ahead of Luther Burden and Colston Loveland, who see more volume but much less per throw.

The raw totals hide a few things. His TD rate ranks just 27th, but he is clean in the red zone (five TDs, no picks, a 12.0 CPOE there), so that number should come up rather than signal a problem. The intermediate band carries the risk: 45.8% completions, a negative CPOE and three of his five interceptions on 48 attempts, even though the big gains there keep its EPA strong. The interception spike in the last three games is almost entirely Week 9 against Tampa Bay, the league's No. 2 defense, where he threw four. His only other bad day came against No. 1 Minnesota in Week 2. His rushing has also faded from a weapon into an occasional escape hatch. Designed runs are getting stuffed 62.5% of the time, while scrambles still return 0.625 EPA apiece. His sack rate is better than league average, but he is pressured often and holds the ball 3.19 seconds, and the season-ending loss of left tackle Braxton Jones makes that a live issue.

The direction is good. The accuracy gains are backed by a real drop in bad throws, not just friendly catch luck. The schedule's worst defenses produce his best games, and the elite ones expose the intermediate-throw risk. Expect a quarterback who sits comfortably in the league's top dozen in efficiency, with interception variance as the price of how often he attacks 10-19 yards.

strengths.title: Short-area accuracy transformed
strengths.body: His completion rate and CPOE have swung from below average to near the top of the league, and the drop in bad throws shows the change is mechanical, not just receivers bailing him out. Quick, on-schedule throws in Johnson's system are now the base of his game. Some give-back toward the mid-60s is likely, but the bad-throw improvement makes most of this sustainable.

strengths.title: Short throws drive the offense
strengths.body: Throws under 10 air yards are where he builds drives, with a high success rate and strong EPA per attempt rather than empty dump-offs. This is a scheme-plus-skill combination that should hold up against all but the best coverage units.

strengths.title: Scrambles still pay off
strengths.body: He scrambles on 7.9% of dropbacks, and those plays return big EPA and moved the chains nine times. That is the payoff for his long time to throw. The improvising that defined his first two years is now a bonus rather than a crutch.

concerns.title: Intermediate throws invite interceptions
concerns.body: The 10-19 yard band holds three of his five picks and a sub-50% completion rate, even though its big gains keep the EPA healthy. It is partly the cost of an aggressive read, but it is also where good defenses have punished him. Expect this to stay his main risk.

concerns.title: Pressure load without his left tackle
concerns.body: He is pressured on a high share of dropbacks and holds the ball long, and the Bears just lost Braxton Jones for the season. His pressure-to-sack rate has been fine this year, but in 2024 it was among the worst in the league. Protection is the variable most likely to drag the efficiency back down.

concerns.title: Flat when protecting big leads
concerns.body: With the Bears up nine or more, his EPA turns negative and three picks have come in that state. It is partly game script, with conservative calls and forced throws, but it matters for a team about to be a heavy favorite. Designed runs have also been a dead end.

trend.note: His three- and five-game windows are a bit below his season efficiency, but that dip is driven by the four-interception game against No. 2 Tampa Bay. Wins over New England and No. 5 Seattle were efficient and clean. Outside matchups with the two best defenses, the play has been consistent since his Week 6 return.

nextGame.headline: Soft Saints secondary, but their pass rush tests a patched line
nextGame.body:
New Orleans ranks 20th against the pass and 31st on deep throws, and it allows a high rate of explosive passes. That fits the short-to-middle attack and the occasional shot to Odunze, and opposing WR1s have run well above their norms here. The catch is the pass rush: the Saints rank 5th in sack rate, which meets a Bears line without Braxton Jones and a quarterback who holds the ball. The Saints' run defense is 31st, and the Bears are 11.5-point favorites coming off a bye, so heavy rushing late could cap his volume. That is also the game state where his efficiency has sagged.

On the Bears' side, Luther Burden (concussion) is questionable but practicing, and RB Kyle Monangai is aiming to return. Williams himself practiced fully. The Saints are missing two offensive tackles and their center, which hurts their ability to keep pace and strengthens the case for a lopsided script. Linebacker Pete Werner's hamstring could thin their coverage over the middle. An early forecast shows 16 mph wind with gusts near 26, worth watching because it would trim the deep game if it holds.

keyMatchups.title: Odunze against a leaky top-receiver defense
keyMatchups.body: Odunze has been by far his most efficient target, and New Orleans has let opposing WR1s run well above their averages. Combined with the Saints' poor deep-ball defense, this is where explosive plays should come from, wind permitting.

keyMatchups.title: Saints rush vs Jones-less line
keyMatchups.body: New Orleans gets home at a top-five sack rate, and Chicago lost its starting left tackle. How quickly Williams gets the ball out decides whether this is a smooth day or a sack-filled one.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script caps passing volume
keyMatchups.body: A double-digit spread and a 31st-ranked Saints run defense point toward a ground-heavy second half. His EPA has turned negative when leading by nine or more.

nextGame.watch: How fast the ball comes out against the Saints' pass rush with Jones gone. If time to throw stays above three seconds, the sacks will cut into an otherwise favorable matchup.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy gains look durable because they come with a real drop in bad throws and hold across short throws, the red zone and close fourth quarters. Expect his completion rate to settle a little but stay well above his first two seasons. His efficiency should stay around the league's top dozen. The TD rate should drift up given how clean he has been in the red zone, while interceptions should run closer to his first five starts than to the Tampa Bay game. That still leaves more interceptions than last year, because the intermediate aggression is part of the design.

Rushing is the part that has shrunk. Designed runs aren't working, and his scrambles have tapered off, so expect modest ground totals with the occasional big scramble game. A 5-1 team favored by double digits will sometimes protect leads on the ground, which limits his ceiling. Protection without Jones is the biggest threat to the efficiency.
swingFactors: Left-tackle play after Braxton Jones' season-ending injury
Odunze's efficiency holding as his target share grows
How often heavy-favorite scripts turn the offense run-first

confidence.note: Six starts and 195 attempts; the skill change is well supported, but the interception and TD rates rest on small samples.
